analysis.title: Goldman Partner: "Demographics (Multiplied By Agentic Deployment) Are Destiny"
key_insights: Wilson sees US 10y and 30y yields showing near-term exhaustion after a quarter-end flush. Q3 to Q4 portfolio rebalancing and semi-automated flow with limited price sensitivity likely mattered more than usual.

Core PCE came in soft, Fed speakers were more nuanced on the usefulness of imminent hikes, and jobs data showed OK payrolls with no wage pressure. Goldman pushed out its forecast for an October Fed hike.

A disorderly European rates move is the more concerning risk. Wilson cites more complex EU decision-making, a single-objective central bank with limited room to accommodate, French elections next year, and less obvious political leadership.
Goldman's rule of thumb is that equities can absorb a rates move until it reaches 2 standard deviations in a month. Wilson says that threshold was basically hit this week.
Credit is showing spillover from rates. Credit has been under pressure for weeks, HY had its largest 1-day decline in 18 months last week, and credit vol moved sharply this week.

Wilson names two fundamental effects of the yield rise: governments are being forced to recalibrate fiscal plans with fiscal discipline imposed, and central banks have less work to do as financial conditions tighten.
Positioning is already light. Global long/short hedge fund net exposure is in the 5th percentile on a 1-year lookback, 7th on 3-year and 9th on 5-year, and 0%-2% for US equity exposure only.

After two days in Riyadh, Wilson flags that the catalyst calendar into US midterms and Israeli elections could change the Middle East conflict trajectory, with oil flows reportedly back to pre-March levels.
Meta was up 30% in September. Wilson highlights Muse's launch and the consumer use cases accelerating AI adoption, and says the America.gov AI launch could change the perceived AI narrative.

Micron results were good enough to hold the share price near record highs. Meta's September move and early Q4 highs in Nvidia and Nasdaq point to broadening from capex beneficiaries to facilitators of AI use.
Wilson expects narrow breadth to be a feature, not a bug, of the next significant move higher in equities. He notes breadth is already poor.

Wilson argues 'demographics, multiplied by effective agentic deployment, are destiny'. With European social unrest, higher yields and the Super-Intelligence discussions at the White House, he finds it hard to resist US tech over other geographies.

The author's synthesis is that relief and damage are no longer on the same clock: a US rates pause can arrive without becoming an equity bid. The open question is which shock comes first, a disorderly European rates move or the Middle East calendar.

sector_views.rationale: Wilson finds it hard to resist US tech over other geographies, citing AI adoption broadening to use-case facilitators and social unrest in Europe.
Wilson describes himself as a constructive contrarian on European stocks but sees Europe as more vulnerable to a disorderly rates move.
